summary: Help 6–7 year-olds move from recognising shapes by how they look to defining them by their properties. A defining attribute is one a shape must have (a triangle: three straight sides, closed; a square: four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners); a non-defining ('imposed') attribute is incidental (colour, size, overall orientation, sitting on a horizontal base). Children routinely treat imposed attributes as defining — rejecting a rotated square as a 'diamond', or a long-thin or point-down triangle as 'not a real triangle'. The core moves are: contrast varied examples with carefully chosen near-miss non-examples, foreground the invariant defining feature, rotate/resize the same shape to show identity is preserved, and ask children to explain WHY a shape is or is not a given type.
misconceptions: Treats ORIENTATION as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' have a horizontal base — about 15% of children reject even a prototypical triangle once it is rotated.
Treats shape type as defined by its image/prototype: only 'regular' triangles or brick-like rectangles count; long-thin, right and obtuse triangles are rejected.
Thinks size or colour can change a shape's identity (a very big or a red triangle is 'a different shape').
Accepts a near-miss non-example (a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle') because it resembles the prototype — ignoring 'straight' and 'closed'.

activities.title: Triangle studio: what can change, what cannot
steps: Drag the three corners of a triangle to stretch it into different types (long-thin, right, obtuse) and tilt it to any angle, checking after each change whether it is still a triangle and saying why (if the three corners are dragged into one straight line, it flattens and is no longer a triangle).
Use size and colour controls to make the triangle big, small, and recoloured, and confirm the label 'triangle' stays the same because three straight sides and closure have not changed.

Break the shape on purpose: bend one side into a curve, or drag a corner apart so the outline no longer closes, and watch the label flip to 'not a triangle' with the non-straight side or the open gap highlighted.
State in your own words which attributes can be 'thrown around' with no effect (colour, size, orientation) and which changes end it (for example a curved side or an open corner).
activities.insight: Size, colour and orientation can swing wildly while a shape keeps its identity, but the instant a side curves or a corner opens it stops being a triangle — this makes defining versus non-defining attributes directly visible.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and explain why
steps: Decide for each drawn figure whether it is or is not a given shape: non-prototypical positives (long-thin triangle, point-down triangle, tilted square) and near-miss negatives (one curved side, an open/unclosed corner).

For every decision, justify it by naming the defining property — e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up' or 'that side isn't straight' — rather than 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.
Compare a figure with one resized/recoloured and state whether anything that matters has changed.

Trace a finger along each side of a borderline figure to test 'how many sides?', 'is every side straight?' and 'is it joined up all the way round?' (and, for a square, 'are all four sides equal and all four corners square?')
activities.insight: Membership of a shape category depends on invariant defining properties, and the reason given — not just the yes/no — shows whether a child is reasoning from properties or from the prototype.

activities.title: Shape detective: argue back
steps: Respond to a character who holds up a rotated square and insists 'that's a diamond, not a square', arguing back from the four equal sides and square corners.
Answer repeated 'how do you know it's a triangle?' challenges, citing a defining attribute each time until the character concedes.
Handle thrown counterexamples — a curved-sided or unclosed figure — by explaining exactly which defining feature is missing.
Defend why size and colour changes do not change the shape's name.
activities.insight: Being able to defend a classification out loud with the defining attribute, against a plausible prototype-based objection, is the goal — the reasoning is what is being learned.

activities.title: Build and draw to a defining spec
steps: Draw a triangle that looks completely different from a given one but is still a triangle (e.g. long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down), then explain why it still counts.
Build shapes from sticks or strips to a spec such as 'three straight sides, joined up all the way round'.
Make a near-miss on purpose (leave a corner open, or use a bendy side) and say what would have to change to fix it.
Turn your own cut-out shape, and compare it with a larger or smaller version, checking aloud that the defining attributes stay the same.
activities.insight: Producing a novel valid example — and justifying it — shows the child can apply the defining properties rather than only recognise a tidy prototype.

activities.title: Must-have versus doesn't-matter reference
steps: Reveal a shape's must-have attributes (three straight sides, closed) and its doesn't-matter attributes (colour, size, orientation) shown greyed out, and read which column each feature belongs to.
Sort a few new attributes into 'must-have' or 'doesn't-matter' using the panel as a guide.
After consulting the panel, decide a fresh borderline case and say which column your reason came from.
activities.insight: Keeping an explicit two-column picture of defining versus incidental attributes supports children in checking their reasoning against the right criteria.

checkQuestion: Show the child three figures in turn: a long, thin triangle; a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom; and a near-miss with one gently curved side. For each ask 'Is this a triangle? How do you know?' Then show a square rotated 45° and ask 'Is this a square, or something else? Why?'
checkAnswer: The long-thin and point-down figures ARE triangles (three straight sides, closed) whatever their proportions or orientation; the curved-sided figure is NOT (a side isn't straight); the rotated square IS still a square (four equal straight sides, four right-angle corners) — turning it does not change what it is. Reasons cite the defining attributes, not the look or the base.
